title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, and which languages you speak — and see for the first time that English prepositions turn into word endings in Finnish.
bekal: answer *mistä* (where from) and *missä* (where) with the endings *-sta/-stä* and *-ssa/-ssä*
turn a country name into a nationality and a language name — one root, three faces
attach the six person endings to a verb without needing the pronoun

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kahvitauko
dialogs.intro: A coffee break between two classes. Aino and Budi sit in the cafeteria with Marek, a new student from Poland.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Hei! Minä olen Marek. Mistä sinä olet kotoisin?
lines.id: Hi! I'm Marek. Where are you from?
lines.literal: hi! I am Marek. from-what you are originally?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minä olen Indonesiasta. Tarkemmin sanottuna Jakartasta.
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. From Jakarta, to be exact.
lines.literal: I am from-Indonesia. more-precisely said from-Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ai, Jakartasta! Onko se iso kaupunki?
lines.id: Oh, from Jakarta! Is it a big city?
lines.literal: oh, from-Jakarta! is-? it big city?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kyllä, se on erittäin iso. Entä sinä? Mistä sinä olet?
lines.id: Yes, it's very big. And you? Where are you from?
lines.literal: yes, it is very big. and you? from-what you are?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Minä olen Puolasta, Krakovasta. Nyt minä asun Helsingissä.
lines.id: I'm from Poland, from Kraków. Now I live in Helsinki.
lines.literal: I am from-Poland, from-Kraków. now I live in-Helsinki.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Minä asun myös Helsingissä, Kalliossa. Missä sinä asut, Budi?
lines.id: I live in Helsinki too, in Kallio. Where do you live, Budi?
lines.literal: I live also in-Helsinki, in-Kallio. in-what you live, Budi?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minä asun Espoossa. Mitä kieltä sinä puhut kotona, Marek?
lines.id: I live in Espoo. What language do you speak at home, Marek?
lines.literal: I live in-Espoo. what language you speak at-home, Marek?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Puolaa, tietysti. Ja englantia työssä. Puhutko sinä indonesiaa?
lines.id: Polish, of course. And English at work. Do you speak Indonesian?
lines.literal: Polish, of-course. and English at-work. speak-? you Indonesian?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Puhun indonesiaa ja javaa. Ja nyt vähän suomea!
lines.id: I speak Indonesian and Javanese. And now a little Finnish!
lines.literal: speak-I Indonesian and Javanese. and now a-little Finnish!

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Hienoa! Suomi on vaikea kieli, mutta sinä opit nopeasti.
lines.id: Great! Finnish is a hard language, but you learn fast.
lines.literal: great! Finnish is difficult language, but you learn quickly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kiitos! Mutta kielioppi on kyllä vaikeaa.
lines.id: Thanks! But the grammar really is hard.
lines.literal: thanks! but grammar is indeed difficult.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Meille kaikille. Kahvi on kuitenkin hyvää — se auttaa!
lines.id: For all of us. Luckily the coffee is good — that helps!
lines.literal: to-us to-all. coffee is however good — it helps!

notes: **Mistä and missä aren't two separate words to memorize.** They're the same word (*mi-* = what) with different endings: *-stä* means "out of", *-ssä* means "in". The very same endings later attach to nouns: *Helsingi**stä*** (from Helsinki), *Helsingi**ssä*** (in Helsinki). This is the most important pattern in the whole unit.

**A country name becomes three things.** *Suomi* is the country, *suomalainen* the person, *suomea* the language. *Puola → puolalainen → puolaa*. *Indonesia → indonesialainen → indonesiaa*. Once this pattern sinks in, you get three words every time you learn one country.

**Language names always take the partitive form.** *Puhun suome**a***, not *puhun suomi*. This *-a/-ä* ending is called the **partitive**, and it appears because speaking a language means using a part of it, never all of it. For now, just memorize the form; the reason is covered fully in Unit 11.

**Language names are lowercase, country names are capitalized.** *Suomi* (Finland) but *suomi* (Finnish); *Puola* but *puolaa*. Nationalities are lowercase too: *suomalainen*, *indonesialainen*. Compare English, which capitalizes them all.

**The pronoun can disappear.** Look at line 9: *Puhun indonesiaa* — no *minä*. The ending *-n* already says "I", so the pronoun is redundant. Finns drop it all the time for *minä*, *sinä*, *me*, *te*. Not for *hän* and *he*.

**Helsingissä, not Helsinkissä.** The *nk* weakens to *ng* as soon as an ending is attached — this is the consonant gradation whose table you saw in the pronunciation chapter. Compare *Espoo → Espoossa* (nothing weakens, because there's no k/p/t).

grammars.title: -ssa / -ssä and -sta / -stä — "in" and "from"
body: The first two of the fifteen case endings. They come as a pair and are best learned together, because they differ in only one way: one stays inside a place, the other comes out of it.
after: Choose *a* or *ä* by vowel harmony, just as with *-ko/-kö*: *talossa* but *kylässä*. Words whose only vowels are *e* and *i* take the front form — hence *Helsingissä*.

⚠️ *Suomi* first changes to *Suome-* before taking the ending. Nouns ending in *-i* often swap that *i* for *e*: *Suomi → Suomessa*, *nimi → nimessä*, *kieli → kielessä*. It's a pattern, not an exception.
English puts "in" and "from" **before** the word; Finnish attaches them **after** it. The meaning is identical. What needs practice isn't understanding it but the reflex of putting it at the end.

grammars.title: Person endings on verbs
body: Every Finnish verb uses the same six endings. Learn them once and they work for thousands of verbs — including ones you've never seen.
after: The *hän* form is the strangest one: there's no ending at all, **the last vowel is simply lengthened**. *Hän puhuu* — with a long *u*. If you say it short (*hän puhu*), what comes out isn't a wrong sentence but an unfinished one.
The dictionary form (*puhua*, *asua*) is never used as-is in a sentence — it always loses its *-a/-ä* first. What's left (*puhu-*, *asu-*) is the stem the endings attach to.

⚠️ Some verbs change their consonant when a person ending is added — *lukea* (to read) becomes *luen*, not *luken*. That pattern gets its own treatment in Unit 8; for now, use the verbs in this unit as they are.

blocks.text: This table saves you more time than it looks: each row gives you three words at once, and the pattern holds almost without exception.

⚠️ One trap catches every beginner: **Suomi** with a capital letter is the country, **suomi** in lowercase is the language. The sentence *Suomi on Suomessa* makes no sense; *Suomi on kaunis maa* (Finland is a beautiful country) does.

The ending **-lainen/-läinen** means "person from", and it works for cities too: *helsinkiläinen* (someone from Helsinki), *tamperelainen* (someone from Tampere), *jakartalainen*. It doesn't change for gender — men and women are both *suomalainen*.
Nine question words cover nearly everything you need at A1. Notice that the first three are the same word with different place endings — so you're really memorizing only six.

blocks.title: If you only have time to memorize three
items: *Missä?* — where. The one you'll need most as a newcomer.
*Paljonko?* — how much is it. Not a true question word but *paljon* (much) plus the question ending, yet it saves you in every shop.
*Anteeksi, mitä?* — "sorry, what?". The phrase learners use most, and nobody minds hearing it.
What language do you speak at home?
I speak Indonesian and a little Finnish.
